study_identification_part.si4_title: Investigating dopaminergic abnormalities in schizophrenia and first-episode psychosis with normative modelling and multisite molecular neuroimaging

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To demonstrate the feasibility of applying normative modelling (NM) to molecular neuroimaging (PET) in schizophrenia and psychotic disorders, addressing challenges of small sample sizes and diverse experimental designs. The study aimed to: 1) extend analysis of dopamine alterations from striatum to whole brain, 2) identify common patterns of dopamine dysfunction across multiple independent datasets, and 3) link individual deviations from normality to clinical symptoms and treatment response.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: ComBat harmonization (NeuroCombat python library v.0.2.10+) was applied to remove scanner/site batch effects. Batch variable: scanner/site. Covariates preserved during ComBat harmonization: age, sex for both tracers; additionally BMI for [11C]-(+)-PHNO. The study compared three conditions: 1) no harmonization, 2) Gaussian smoothing (3mm kernel, FSL), and 3) ComBat. ComBat was selected as optimal based on smallest differences in Z-score distribution moments (mean, SD) between scanner types and smallest regional differences in extreme deviation percentages. For [11C]-(+)-PHNO: Combat eliminated scanner-related differences in mean Z-scores (p=n.s.) while smoothing did not (p<0.01). For [18F]FDOPA: Combat showed small scanner effect size (η²=-0.022 for mean, η²=0.094 for SD).
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: Combat is a Bayesian harmonisation method... we employed the NeuroCombat python library (v.0.2.10+) [36, 37] and preselected the same covariates subsequently used for NM (i.e., age, sex for both tracers and BMI for [11C]-(+)-PHNO)... When comparing the averages of the distributions between scanner types, we found statistically significant differences... in the data harmonised with smoothing (r = 0.32 [0.08, 0.55], Z = 2.78, p <0.01), while there were no scanner-related differences in the data harmonised with Combat (r = 0.07 [0.004, 0.29], Z = 0.67, p = n.s.)... Combat returned the smallest differences... For FDOPA a small scanner-related effect size (η² = -0.022, 95% CI: [-0.02, 0.06]) was found in terms of mean z-score distribution (χ² = 0.972, p = n.s), while a moderate effect size (η² = 0.094, 95% CI: [0.02, 0.25]) was found for the standard deviation (χ² = 16.9, p < 0.05).

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Voxel-wise Z-scores quantifying deviation from normative distribution. Extreme deviations defined as: Z > 2 (extreme positive), Z < -2 (extreme negative), |Z| > 2 (total extreme). Summary measures: mean Z-score across voxels; percentage of voxels with extreme positive/negative/total deviations. Risk Ratios (RR) comparing patient vs HC extreme deviation prevalence.

caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: The primary outcome of the NM is a measure of deviation, typically expressed as a Z-score... These maps, expressed in terms of Z-scores, measure the distance of a given data point in relation to the average and standard deviation of the posterior probability, weighted for the subject-specific covariates... extreme deviations were defined using a thresholding approach: Z > 2 for extreme positive deviations, Z < -2 for extreme negative deviations, and |Z| > 2 for total extreme deviations... The four summary scores analysed were the mean Z-score, corresponding to the mean Z-score across voxels for each subject, and three measures of extreme deviations from normality, estimated by counting the percentage of voxels with Z-score > 2... Z-score < -2... or |Z-score| > 2... We also calculated the Risk-Ratios (RR) [64] by counting the number of voxels whose Z-scores showed extreme deviations from normality...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: Voxel-wise two-way ANOVA (group × dataset interaction) on Z-score maps with 5000 permutations using FSL randomise, threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE), and FWE correction (pFWE<0.05). Post-hoc tests on significant clusters using rstatix (R 4.2.1). Non-parametric Schreier-Ray-Hare tests on summary measures (mean Z-score, extreme deviations) to assess group and dataset main effects and interactions, followed by post-hoc Kruskal-Wallis H tests. Risk Ratio (RR) calculations using epitools (R 4.2.1). Spearman correlations between deviation metrics and PANSS scores (positive, negative, general, total) in FDOPA_01 and FDOPA_04 datasets. ROC curve analysis (pROC library, R 4.2.1) to assess treatment response prediction using striatal and whole-brain deviation metrics compared to standard Ki measures; DeLong test for ROC curve comparisons. Imaging-transcriptomics analysis (imaging-transcriptomics toolbox) with GSEA on GO Molecular Function gene sets to identify biological pathways associated with spatial deviation patterns.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief:
Answer: Patients with psychosis showed ~2-3 fold increased extreme FDOPA deviations compared to controls (RR: 2.19-2.60), with heterogeneous spatial patterns and minimal inter-patient overlap (<20%). ComBat harmonization effectively reduced scanner/site effects. Striatal FDOPA deviation scores predicted treatment response with AUC 0.77-0.83, comparable to standard Ki analysis. Significant correlations between deviations and PANSS symptoms were found in chronic patients. FEP showed increased positive deviations while chronic SCZ showed increased negative cortical deviations.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: Harmonization: ComBat eliminated scanner-related Z-score distribution differences for [11C]-(+)-PHNO (p=n.s. for mean) and showed small effect sizes for [18F]FDOPA (η²=-0.022 for mean, η²=0.094 for SD), outperforming smoothing and no harmonization. Model performance: FDOPA NM explained up to 15% variance in dopamine synthesis capacity using age and sex; ~56% of GM voxels had EXPV<0 (non-convergence). Deviation patterns: Patients showed significantly elevated Risk Ratios for extreme deviations: RRpos=2.19 (95% CI: 1.97-3.45, p<0.001); RRneg=1.92 (95% CI: 1.60-3.00, p<0.001); RRtot=2.60 (95% CI: 1.36-2.70, p<0.001). Group-level distributions showed small mean difference (|ΔμHC-PAT|=0.14) but larger SD difference (|ΔσHC-PAT|=0.28). Maximum patient overlap in extreme deviations: ~20% in frontal/temporal cortex. Spatial analyses: Voxel-wise group×dataset interaction (Fpeak=21.71, pFWE<0.001) spanning temporal, orbitofrontal, and frontal lobes. Post-hoc: FEP showed greater positive deviations vs HC (FDOPA_01: t=4.92, p<<0.001); chronic SCZ showed greater negative deviations vs HC (FDOPA_02: t=2.22, p<0.05; FDOPA_03: t=4.62, p<0.001). Group effect on total extreme deviations (Fpeak=34.36, pFWE<0.001) localized to left frontal orbital cortex, frontal pole, inferior temporal cortex. Summary measures: Significant group×dataset interaction for mean Z-score (H=9.66, p<0.01); FEP increased mean Z-score (χ²=8.44, p<0.01, η²=0.089); chronic SCZ decreased mean Z-score (FDOPA_03: χ²=7.03, p<0.01, η²=0.177). Main group effects for extreme deviations: positive (H=18.06, p<<0.001, η²=0.101); negative (H=9.51, p<0.01, η²=0.117); total (H=26.52, p<<0.001, η²=0.208). Clinical correlations: FDOPA_04 showed significant Spearman correlations between deviation metrics and PANSS: mean Z-score vs PANSS total (ρ=0.43, p<0.01); total extreme deviations vs PANSS positive (ρ=0.33, p<0.05), negative (ρ=0.39, p<0.01), general (ρ=0.44, p<0.01), total (ρ=0.46, p<0.01). Three clusters (frontal orbital cortex/frontal pole/inferior frontal gyrus; middle temporal gyrus) showed significant correlations with PANSS total (ρ=0.36-0.43, all p<0.05). FDOPA_01 (FEP) showed correlation between total extreme deviations and PANSS negative (ρ=0.47, p<0.05). Treatment response prediction: Striatal mean Z-score ROC AUCs: FDOPA_01=0.83, FDOPA_02=0.77, FDOPA_03=0.83; comparable to standard striatal Ki (AUCs: 0.83, 0.79, 0.74 respectively; no significant differences by DeLong test). Whole-brain deviation scores did not significantly predict treatment response except FDOPA_02 negative extreme deviations (AUC=0.72). Transcriptomics: Enriched gene sets associated with deviation patterns included 'structural constituent of ribosome' (NES=2.49, pFDR<0.05), 'neurotransmitter receptor activity' (NES=2.18, pFDR<0.05), 'glutamate receptor activity' (NES=2.04, pFDR<0.05).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: This study demonstrates the first application of normative modeling to molecular neuroimaging (PET) for psychiatric disorders, addressing unique challenges of small sample sizes, high costs, and multi-scanner data in molecular imaging. Key innovations include: 1) Systematic evaluation of harmonization methods for multi-scanner PET data; 2) Successful application to patient-only cohorts without matched controls (FDOPA_04), demonstrating clinical feasibility; 3) Integration with automatic FDOPA kinetic modeling pipeline for standardized processing; 4) Use of imaging-transcriptomics to link spatial deviation patterns to biological pathways; 5) Demonstration that NM-derived striatal measures can predict treatment response comparably to standard kinetic analysis. The approach could reduce the need for matched controls in future studies, decreasing costs and radiation exposure. Authors suggest this framework is generalizable to other PET/SPECT tracers and neuropsychiatric disorders. Limitations of voxel-wise approach with high non-convergence rate suggest ROI-based modeling may be more practical for molecular imaging applications.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Discussion section provides detailed consideration of methodological innovations, clinical applications, and future directions for normative modeling in molecular neuroimaging.
Supporting Text: our primary objective is to demonstrate the feasibility of employing normative modelling for molecular neuroimaging in SCZ and psychotic disorders... our study explored the feasibility of investigating dopaminergic alterations of [18F]FDOPA without acquiring a matched set of healthy controls... integrating a normative reference population could significantly reduce, if not eliminate, the need to acquire matched healthy controls (HC) in future research studies... along with automatic standardised frameworks for kinetic modelling of [18F]FDOPA [52], represents a significant step forward in establishing PET parametric imaging as a quantitative companion tool for clinical management... our results encourage the adoption of this analytical framework to any molecular target measured by PET or SPECT neuroimaging and in other neuropsychiatric disorders.

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: 1) Modest explained variance (15% for FDOPA, 30% for PHNO) with substantial non-convergence (~56% GM voxels EXPV<0 for FDOPA), likely due to limited sample sizes and PET signal-to-noise characteristics. 2) Residual scanner/site differences exist in higher-order statistics (skewness, kurtosis) despite ComBat harmonization. 3) ComBat assumes linear scanner effects, which may not hold for tomographs with different geometries. 4) Voxel-level modeling is sensitive to noise; regional modeling might improve performance but was avoided to prevent parcellation bias. 5) Heterogeneous clinical samples with missing clinical information for some individuals limited statistical power. 6) Sample size modest compared to MRI normative modeling studies (recommendation: ≥50 HC total; ≥10 per site for multi-site). 7) Datasets included both FEP and SCZ which are distinct nosological entities; FEP cohorts may include affective psychosis or unspecified psychosis, contributing to heterogeneity. 8) Cannot establish causality regarding differential FEP vs chronic SCZ patterns (disease duration vs medication effects). 9) Treatment response definitions varied across datasets.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Discussion section provides extensive detailed limitations covering methodological, statistical, clinical, and interpretational issues.
Supporting Text: This work is subject to several limitations. Firstly, the modelling process is influenced by the harmonization method and may not account for non-linearities... residual differences still exist in the datasets when assessed with statistics of the second order or above (e.g., skewness, kurtosis). Secondly, applying NM at the voxel level can result in underperformance of the model due to high noise and poor signal. Consequently, there are a considerable number of voxels where the model fails to converge... Thirdly, the deviation scores might be sensitive to motion [98]... Fourthly, the heterogeneity of the clinical sample used in the analysis and the presence of missing clinical information for some individuals... Even if our dataset can be considered a large one for a molecular neuroimaging study, it is indeed modest compared to normative modelling MRI studies... for [18F]FDOPA PET we recommend a reference 50 scans and in case of multiple scans/sites, at least 10 normative subjects each... Another limitation is that our datasets included patients with SCZ and FEP, which are distinct nosological entities... we cannot establish whether this differential pattern between FEP and chronic patients is attributed to variances in disease duration or is linked to medication effects... the definition of treatment response varied across datasets.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is the first published application of normative modeling to molecular neuroimaging (PET). The study pools [11C]-(+)-PHNO data from 2 studies (77 HC) and [18F]FDOPA data from 142 HC and 109 patients across multiple previous studies from 3 imaging sites with 5 different scanners. Full scanner details: [11C]-(+)-PHNO acquired on Siemens Hi-Rez Biograph 6 (PET/CT, n=54) and Siemens Biograph mMR (PET/MR, n=23) at Invicro, London. [18F]FDOPA acquired on Siemens Hi-Rez Biograph 6, Siemens Biograph 40 TruePoint, Siemens TruePoint 6, ECAT HR+962, and ECAT EXACT 3D at MRC Cyclotron Unit (London), Invicro (London), and Bundang Hospital (South Korea). All FDOPA scans used pre-medication with carbidopa (150mg) and entacapone (400mg) 1h before scanning. Acquisition protocol: ~90 min dynamic scan starting at tracer injection; injected dose 86.4-414.4 MBq. The study demonstrates that ComBat harmonization is superior to Gaussian smoothing for removing multi-scanner/site effects in PET data. PCNToolkit v1.20.0 was used with default non-informative Bayesian priors and Powell optimizer. Grey matter masking at 30% probability threshold yielded 199,715 voxels per tracer. The FDOPA normative model showed substantial non-convergence (~56% voxels EXPV<0), requiring EXPV>3% threshold for main analyses (preserving 26.18% of original GM mask). The study included treatment response analyses for three datasets with varying response criteria: FDOPA_01 used >50% PANSS reduction sustained ≥6 months; FDOPA_02 used Remission Working Group criteria (remitters) vs modified Kane criteria (treatment-resistant); FDOPA_03 used ≥2 weeks first-line antipsychotic without clozapine history (responders) vs non-response to ≥2 first-line drugs. FDOPA_04 response criteria: CGI-SCH<4, PANSS total<60, compliance>3, ≤1 medication change due to adverse events (responders) vs ≥2 medications >4 weeks each, CGI-SCH>30, PANSS>70, compliance>3 (non-responders). PANSS scores were available for FDOPA_01 and FDOPA_04 subsets only. The imaging-transcriptomics analysis used the Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression data to map F-statistic spatial patterns to enriched gene sets. This study represents a proof-of-concept that normative modeling can be applied to molecular neuroimaging despite unique challenges of limited sample sizes, high inter-subject variability, and multi-scanner effects in PET data.
